learn.canDo: Choose between prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning from the failure you measure, and combine retrieval for facts with tuning for format.
learn.why: 'Should we fine-tune?' is the most common wrong question. Knowing what each tool is for saves months.
learn.keyIdea: Retrieval changes what it answers from; tuning changes how.

learn.canDo: Explain low-rank adapters, choose rank and target layers, and use QLoRA to fit a job on a small GPU.
learn.why: Parameter-efficient tuning is how most teams fine-tune. Knowing the dials shows you have done it.
learn.keyIdea: A habit is a small change to a big skill.

learn.canDo: Compute model size from bits, explain why smaller is faster, and pick a bit width and method by measuring quality.
learn.why: Quantization decides what you can serve and at what cost. Knowing the knee in the curve is practical judgement.
learn.keyIdea: Size is arithmetic; quality is what you buy with it.

learn.canDo: Work out whether a model fits a GPU from weights, key-value cache and overhead, and choose bits, context and offload to make it fit.
learn.why: Context length costs memory, not only tokens. This is the question behind every local setup.
learn.keyIdea: Weights are only part of what you hold.

chapter.story: The team asks whether to fine-tune a model, and whether it could run on their own hardware.
outcomes: Pick between prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning
Tune a model cheaply with adapters
Fit a model and its context on a small GPU
chapter.why: Prompting is not the only way to change what a model does. Each alternative has a price in effort, memory and quality.
chapter.payoff: In an interview you can say when you would fine-tune and how you would serve it. At work you will size a model for the hardware you have.
